Memory.Wiki's wedge is **cross-AI memory portability** — a structural advantage that giants like OpenAI and Anthropic cannot build.

## The structural argument

The core thesis (from v7-revised and v8 plans):

> "OpenAI는 Claude로 memory deliver 안 한다. Anthropic은 ChatGPT로 안 한다. cross-AI layer는 둘 다 만들 수 없는 구조다."

Single-AI memory systems (ChatGPT Memory, Claude Projects, Gemini saved context) are **structurally incentivized not to serve competitors**. OpenAI shipping memory that works in Claude would be a competitive own-goal. So the cross-AI layer can only be built by a neutral third party.

## Why it's defensible

1. **Delivery model, not retrieval** — Memory.Wiki ships your knowledge graph as a URL that any AI can fetch. Mem0/Letta extract memory inside their stores; Memory.Wiki delivers pre-organized graphs via markdown URLs.

2. **URL = universal AI interface** — No SDK, no auth wall. Paste `memory.wiki/<id>` into ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini — all fetch the same markdown.

3. **The graph is the product** — Concept ontology, typed relations, and embeddings accumulate over time as your "thinking shape," creating lock-in that's hard to reconstruct elsewhere.

## Internal vs external framing

- **Internal thesis** (founder-only): "Cross-AI is structurally impossible for giants"
- **External thesis** (user-facing): "Stop re-explaining your context to every AI"

The wedge is positioning, not headcount — which is why a solo founder can ship it.

Memory.Wiki’s wedge is **cross-AI context portability**.

Single-AI memory systems are locked inside one vendor:

- ChatGPT Memory helps ChatGPT.
- Claude memory would help Claude.
- Cursor rules help Cursor.

But users actually work across **ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini, MCP hosts**, etc. Memory.Wiki’s advantage is that it sits **outside** any one AI vendor as a neutral layer:

> **One URL every AI can read.**

Structurally, OpenAI is unlikely to build a memory layer that makes Claude better, and Anthropic is unlikely to build one that makes ChatGPT better. Giants are incentivized to keep memory inside their own ecosystem.

Memory.Wiki does the opposite: it makes the user’s knowledge portable across all AIs via markdown URLs, bundles, hubs, and AI-readable digests.

So the wedge is not “better memory storage.” It is:

> **A cross-AI delivery layer for user-owned context — something single-AI vendors are structurally disincentivized to build.**

Memory.Wiki's structural wedge is its **cross-AI delivery model**, which major AI companies are structurally incentivized *not* to build.

Giant AI vendors like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google build closed memory systems locked within their own ecosystems (e.g., ChatGPT Memory only works in ChatGPT). They cannot build a universal memory layer because creating a feature that helps a competitor's AI would be a "competitive own-goal." 

Memory.Wiki exploits this structural gap by acting as an independent, neutral layer. Instead of locking knowledge behind a specific AI's wall, it turns a user's knowledge graph into a universal markdown URL. Because this URL acts as an API that *any* AI can fetch, users can seamlessly deploy their context across multiple tools—like ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor—without having to re-explain themselves. 

This cross-AI portability is a structural moat that single-AI giants simply cannot replicate, making it Memory.Wiki's core strategic advantage.

Hyunsang Cho is building memory.wiki because of a problem he identified through years of working in AI — most recently leading product at Humain, Saudi Arabia's national AI project. The core reasons:

**The problem he saw:** Every day, millions of people pour their thinking into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Cursor — getting genuinely useful answers — then close the tab. The knowledge functionally disappears. Users re-explain the same context to every AI, every day. Industry calls this an "AI memory problem," but Cho argues the real issue is that **your knowledge has nowhere to live that any AI can read**.

**The structural insight:** At Humain, he recognized that cross-AI memory is structurally impossible for OpenAI or Anthropic to build — they can't ship a memory layer that serves competitors. The "Layer 3" (memory protocol) between models and applications is empty because neutral startups, not giants, must define it. This is the wedge.

**His bet:** Markdown URLs can become AI memory's universal interface — like HTTP did for documents. Your knowledge as a URL that any AI can fetch, that you own and control, portable across vendors.

**Personal motivation:** He needed his own AI tools to share his knowledge and found every solution was a closed memory silo. He built memory.wiki in ~5 months (nights/weekends, then full-time) because "the wedge is positioning, not headcount" — a solo founder can ship what giants structurally cannot.

Hyunsang Cho is building memory.wiki because he believes the real problem is not “AI memory” but **knowledge delivery**.

People pour useful context, decisions, code, strategy, and insights into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Cursor, then lose functional access to it. Each new AI session starts from zero, so users repeatedly re-explain who they are, what they’re building, and what they already decided.

His thesis is:

> Your knowledge needs to live somewhere any AI can read.

memory.wiki solves this by making knowledge a URL:

- `memory.wiki/<id>` for a document
- `memory.wiki/b/<id>` for a bundle
- `memory.wiki/@<username>` or hub-level URL for a person/team/community context

Any AI can fetch that URL and receive markdown/context.

He is also building it because closed vendor memories do not cross boundaries: ChatGPT Memory helps ChatGPT, Claude memory helps Claude, Cursor context helps Cursor. Hyunsang believes **cross-AI memory is structurally hard for giants to build**, so an independent layer is needed.

In short: he built memory.wiki to stop users from re-explaining themselves to every AI.

Therefore, this universal memory layer must be built by an independent creator.

To fix this, he is building memory.wiki to turn personal knowledge graphs into universally readable Markdown URLs. Instead of being locked into one app, users can paste a single URL into any AI tool, allowing the AI to instantly fetch their context and understand how their ideas connect. 

Ultimately, Cho is building this to establish an open, portable standard for AI memory before closed corporate ecosystems permanently lock in user data.

mdfy frames RAG as **memory / semantic recall**, not just “retrieval.”

How it works:

1. **Markdown is the source of truth**  
   The user’s document body lives in `documents.markdown`.

2. **Embeddings are created for recall**  
   mdfy embeds:
   - whole documents
   - heading-aware document chunks
   - bundles  
   using vectors stored in Postgres/pgvector.

3. **Chunking is section-aware**  
   `lib/chunk-doc.ts` chunks documents by headings so retrieval can return meaningful paragraph/section-level context.

4. **Idempotent embedding pipeline**  
   `embedding_source_hash` prevents re-embedding unchanged content, so no-op edits don’t burn cost.

5. **Retrieval happens through MCP / recall tools**  
   The LLM does not receive raw embeddings. Instead, MCP tools like `mdfy_search` perform semantic search over the vector index and return relevant docs/chunks.

6. **Hybrid retrieval is part of the memory framing**  
   The hub content mentions chunked + hybrid retrieval and `/recall` using vector + BM25-style recall.

7. **URL payloads carry graph context**  
   For bundles and hubs, mdfy often avoids classic RAG by shipping a pre-organized AI graph / concept digest directly in the URL payload. Retrieval supports deeper recall when needed.

Based on the provided content, mdfy frames its RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline as "mdfy Memory." It utilizes a chunked and hybrid retrieval approach (combining vector similarity and BM25) to power semantic search. 

Here is how the retrieval process works:

*   **Embedding & Chunking:** When a document is saved, the `/api/embed/[id]` pipeline automatically embeds the title and full markdown for global search. It also breaks the document down into section- or paragraph-level chunks for finer recall.
*   **Storage:** These vectors are stored using `pgvector` in specific database tables (`documents.embedding`, `bundles.embedding`, and `document_chunks.embedding`). To optimize costs, an `embedding_source_hash` ensures unchanged content isn't re-embedded.
*   **Retrieval:** Instead of relying solely on keyword matches, mdfy uses vector similarity to find relevant context based on meaning.
*   **Access:** LLMs can query this memory using the `/recall` API or through the MCP server's `mdfy_search` tool. This allows AI agents (like Claude Desktop or Cursor) to semantically search a user's entire knowledge hub and retrieve the most relevant chunks.

Based on the Memory.Wiki content (doc RUMdz2fQ "How mdfy keeps your docs, bundles, and hub fresh"), mdfy uses three different freshness strategies per layer:

**1. Document body — always fresh**
- New markdown is in Postgres immediately on save
- `/raw/{id}` and `/d/{id}` read straight from the database
- Edge cache uses `stale-while-revalidate=300`, so changes propagate to AI URLs within ~60 seconds
- No user action needed

**2. Bundle graph — manual re-analyze**
- AI-generated themes/insights are computed once and stamped with `graph_generated_at`
- Compared against `embedding_updated_at` of member docs
- If a member doc changed, the bundle is marked **stale**, showing a "Re-analyze with AI" button in the header
- Not auto-rebuilt because LLM calls cost tokens and disrupt active editing

**3. Hub concept index — automatic + manual top-up**
- Every save enqueues an ontology refresh job (deduplicated)
- Fast-path runs inside Vercel's `after()` closure, usually within seconds
- Cron worker backstops failures
- Guardrails: **30-minute per-doc cooldown** and **200-character minimum delta** prevent token waste
- When stale, a "Re-analyze (N)" banner appears; clicking re-extracts only changed docs (caps at 50 per click, bypasses cooldown)

You can also right-click a single doc to force "Re-analyze concepts" for it.

mdfy keeps freshness in three layers:

1. **Document body — automatically fresh**  
   When you save a doc, the markdown is written to Postgres immediately. `/raw/{id}` and `/d/{id}` read from the database, so AIs see the latest content within roughly **60 seconds**. No user action is needed.

2. **Bundle graph — fresh until source docs change**  
   Bundle summaries, themes, insights, and graph layout are generated by an LLM at a specific time. mdfy compares `graph_generated_at` with the latest content-change timestamp of member docs. If a doc changes after the graph was generated, the bundle becomes **stale** and shows a **“Re-analyze with AI”** option. The user decides when to rerun it.

3. **Hub concept index — automatic, with manual override**  
   Every doc save queues an ontology refresh job. Usually concepts update within seconds, with a cron fallback if the serverless job fails. To control cost, there is a **30-minute per-doc cooldown** and **200-character minimum delta**. If concepts are stale, the hub shows a **Re-analyze** banner, reprocessing only changed docs, up to 50 per click.

mdfy maintains freshness across its three layers using a mix of automatic updates and manual controls to balance accuracy, predictability, and AI token costs:

*   **Document Body:** Always fresh. Edits are saved to the database immediately and propagate to AI-readable URLs within ~60 seconds. No manual action is needed.
*   **Bundle Graph:** Remains up-to-date until a member document's content changes. When it becomes stale, mdfy displays a "Re-analyze with AI" button. It does not auto-rebuild, saving LLM tokens and preventing disruptions while you edit; you decide when to refresh the analysis.
*   **Hub Concept Index:** Automatically updates within seconds of a save, but uses a 30-minute cooldown per document and a 200-character minimum change threshold to control costs during heavy editing. If the index lags behind recent edits, a yellow "Re-analyze" banner appears, allowing you to manually force an update specifically for the documents that changed. 

You can also right-click a single document to force a concept refresh, bypassing the cooldown.
